Newly hatched neonates of the waterflea Leydigia ciliata emerge from the brood chamber with a total length at birth of 0.0370 centimeters [Lb = 0.0370 centimeters], placing them among the smaller-bodied offspring within the Chydoridae family. This modest initial size reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo during its brief incubation period within the maternal carapace. The age at which these neonates are released has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions, with the time since birth at birth recorded as 1.87 days [ab = 1.87 days], a value consistent with the rapid embryogenesis observed in other small-bodied cladocerans. Following their liberation into the water column, the young individuals must quickly initiate filter feeding on suspended bacteria and detritus to sustain their growth trajectory. The population growth dynamics of this species are strongly influenced by these early life-history parameters, as a smaller body size at birth generally correlates with a longer juvenile period and higher vulnerability to invertebrate predators. Field surveys in littoral zones have reported that newly released neonates are often found in association with fine particulate organic matter, suggesting a microhabitat preference that may reduce predation risk during this critical phase of development.

The developmental progression from birth to the onset of reproductive capability in Leydigia ciliata occurs over a relatively compressed time frame when the animals are reared at a constant temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the time since birth at puberty is a mere 2.75 days [tp = 2.75 days], indicating a remarkably swift maturation process characteristic of many ephemeral habitat specialists. at a temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]Reaching the total length at puberty of 0.0547 centimeters [Lp = 0.0547 centimeters] triggers the onset of gametogenesis, after which females begin producing their first clutch of subitaneous eggs. This rapid attainment of maturity is hypothesized to be an adaptive response to the unpredictable drying cycles of the temporary ponds and shallow littoral zones this species inhabits. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that such a short pre-reproductive period is unusual, as most Leydigia species require approximately four to six days to reach a comparable developmental stage at similar temperatures. The energetic investment required to achieve this accelerated maturation likely comes at the cost of reduced somatic growth, a life-history trade-off that may limit the ultimate body size attainable by individuals in these populations.

As individuals of Leydigia ciliata continue to develop past the pubertal molt, they approach their ultimate total length of 0.089 centimeters [Li = 0.089 centimeters], a measurement that represents the asymptotic body size for this species under optimal food conditions. This maximum length, while modest in absolute terms, is typical for members of the Chydoridae subfamily Aloninae and reflects constraints imposed by the mechanical limits of the carapace exoskeleton. The corresponding ultimate dry weight has been estimated at 8.35 micrograms , a value that scales geometrically from the linear measurement based on allometric relationships established for related daphniids. Attainment of this final body size typically coincides with the peak of the reproductive period, after which somatic growth effectively ceases and all available resources are channeled into egg production. The relationship between ultimate length and dry weight is particularly relevant for bioenergetic modeling of secondary production in benthic communities, where Leydigia ciliata can contribute substantially to the turnover of detrital biomass. Specimens approaching this maximum size are frequently observed in the final instars of their development, their larger carapaces offering a greater filtering surface area for particle collection.

The reproductive output of mature females is tightly coupled to the prevailing water temperature, with maximum rates achieved under the same thermal regime that accelerates earlier development. At 29 °C [T = 29 °C], a reproductively active female exhibits a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.46 neonates per day [Ri = approximately 0.46 neonates per day], reflecting the species' strategy of producing relatively few, well-provisioned offspring rather than numerous small eggs. These 20 neonates are distributed across a reproductive window spanning the interval from puberty to the end of life, with the maximum reproduction rate estimated from the ratio of total offspring produced to the duration of the reproductive period. The relative scarcity of neonates per brood compared to larger daphniids is offset by the higher survival probability of each individual, as the larger egg size confers greater initial energy reserves. Field collections from productive littoral habitats have confirmed that ovigerous females bearing multiple eggs in their brood chambers are most abundant during the warm summer months, when water temperatures routinely approach this optimal thermal threshold. The quality of suspended particulate matter also plays a modulating role, with females fed on bacteria-rich diets producing more broods over a longer period than those subsisting on detrital particles alone.

Longevity in Leydigia ciliata is constrained by the same metabolic demands that drive its rapid early development, with individuals reared at 29 °C [T = 29 °C] exhibiting a maximum lifespan of 46 days [am = 46 days]. This relatively short life expectancy is characteristic of small-bodied cladocerans inhabiting temporary or ephemeral water bodies, where the risk of habitat desiccation imposes a selective premium on completing the life cycle quickly. By the end of this lifespan, the cumulative reproductive contribution of each female, when combined with the high survival rates of the large-bodied neonates, ensures that population numbers can rebound quickly following a disturbance event. The 46 day maximum, however, is only realized under constant, favorable conditions; in natural settings, exposure to fluctuating temperatures, food limitation, or predation can substantially truncate this potential longevity. Comparative studies of sediment cores from shallow lakes have revealed that ephippia of Leydigia ciliata are often most abundant in layers corresponding to intermittent wet-dry cycles, suggesting that the species' life-history strategy is finely tuned to exploit brief periods of habitat availability. Even beyond the age of 30 days, reproductively active females may still produce viable clutches, though brood sizes tend to decline as senescence progresses, mirroring patterns observed across the entire crustacean order Diplostraca.
